# Lineages

Data science did not invent the problem of making expertise answer to the public. Journalists, lawyers, accountants, planners, and engineers each faced a version of it decades ago, usually after a failure that embarrassed the profession in public: an exposé that could not be checked, a right that existed only on paper, an audit that blessed a fraud, a highway that split a neighborhood, a bridge that fell. Each responded the same way. It did not stop at professing values. It built records, routines, and institutions that made the values hard to ignore. Keegan [-@keegan2026] calls this infrastructuring, and Part I named what it produces: the installed base of linkability, interpretability, continuity, safe scrutiny, authority, and remedy (@sec-ch-02-installed-base).

Part II reads those five professions as instruction manuals. Each chapter takes one lineage, names the element of the installed base it is best at building, and turns its signature practice into a tool you can run.

- **Journalism** (@sec-ch-06-journalism) maintains the evidentiary surface of public life: sourcing, corroboration, right of reply, and publication with documentation. You reproduce a published investigation and see what its open data made possible.
- **Law** (@sec-ch-07-law) translates values into enforceable procedures: rights of access, duties to disclose, and remedies. You read a records statute as machinery and track requests against its clock.
- **Accounting and auditing** (@sec-ch-08-accounting) formalize independent verification through workpapers, standards fixed in advance, and separation from the client. You run a disaggregated audit and turn it into a workpaper someone else can rerun.
- **Planning** (@sec-ch-09-planning) asks who decided, who was affected, and who was in the room, and supplies participatory repertoires for contesting durable systems. You map stakeholders and dockets.
- **Engineering** (@sec-ch-10-engineering) learns from failure through testing, incident review, and high-reliability practice. You put the audit under test and break it on purpose.

Each lineage also has a natural level of government, and the worked examples follow it. Journalism works best at the **city**, where records are abundant and scattered and the local watchdog has thinned. Planning sits at the **county**, which in Colorado writes the comprehensive plan and decides land-use applications for unincorporated land. Law sits at the **state**, because state legislatures write the open-records statutes that bind cities and counties and, increasingly, the laws that govern automated decisions. Accounting and engineering sit at the **nation**, where federal agencies report thousands of AI uses and the government keeps the inventories, audit institutions, and incident boards that assurance needs. The levels are a convention for choosing examples, not a claim that each profession lives at only one. Real problems cross levels, and anchor cases such as COMPAS in a Florida county, Central 70 in Denver, or SyRI in the Netherlands sit wherever they happened.

The chapters can be read in any order. Each names the concepts it relies on and links to where they are developed, and the genres of Part IV (@sec-ch-14-op-eds through @sec-ch-19-archival-deposits) carry each lineage's work to the body that can act on it.

Borrowing from professions has a cost. Every profession has its own pathologies, and borrowing a method means borrowing its blind spots. Accounting's independence norms coexisted with Arthur Andersen, and Lee [-@leeProfessionalizationAccountancyHistory1995] describes the profession's history as protecting the public interest "in a self-interested way" (@sec-ch-08-accounting). Public interest law splits into a well-funded strategic tier and an overstretched front line [@albiston2017]. Planning's confident public interest built Robert Moses's expressways before Davidoff [-@davidoff1965] tried to pluralize it. Engineering's own literature documents how safe systems drift into failure one reasonable decision at a time [@vaughan1996]. Journalism's watchdog depended on a commercial newspaper model that has collapsed [@zengGhostsNewspapersPublic2022]. Professions also gatekeep. Credentials decide who may speak with authority, and Stapleton and colleagues [-@stapletonWhoHasInterest2022] ask who benefits when a field claims the label "public interest" at all.

The chapters treat these pathologies as part of the inheritance, not footnotes to it. Part III (@sec-ch-11-pit-data-for-good through @sec-ch-13-critical-data-studies-refusal) turns to newer conversations that started from different assumptions, and @sec-ch-20-limits asks what the framework cannot see because it was built from these five.
